blocks.label: Customer Support Resolution Agent
blocks.narrative: A Claude Agent SDK support agent grows across this block from raw agentic-loop mechanics through tool API correctness, critical-action safeguards, coordinator prompting, custom commands, error propagation, MCP tooling choices, escalation calibration, session management, and long-conversation reliability.

blocks.label: Developer Productivity with Claude
blocks.narrative: A platform engineering team builds and refines a developer-productivity agent on Claude Code: exploring an unfamiliar internal monorepo, applying path-scoped conventions, generating boilerplate, enforcing release and merge preconditions, and automating dependency and license checks — combining built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) with a handful of custom MCP servers.

blocks.label: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
blocks.narrative: A generic engineering team runs Claude Code inside its CI/CD pipeline to power automated code review, PR feedback, and test generation. Across this block, the pipeline matures from a bare, ad hoc invocation into a properly scoped system: non-interactive execution, schema-guaranteed structured findings, skill-scoped tooling, workload-appropriate use of the Batches API, disciplined CLAUDE.md/rules/Skills organization, careful session management across long-running investigations, and multi-instance review architecture that catches what same-session self-review misses.

blocks.label: Structured Data Extraction
blocks.narrative: A recruiting-operations team builds a pipeline that extracts structured candidate records — job history, education, certifications, skills, compensation expectations — from submitted resumes and application forms into a validated JSON schema. The block follows the pipeline in sequence: schema design and its fabrication risks, the coordinator-subagent architecture that runs it, semantic-vs-syntax validation and retry-with-feedback, then the context-management and human-oversight layers that keep long documents, batches, and interactive correction sessions reliable.

questions.stem: Your support agent's response sometimes pairs a short acknowledgment — 'Let me check that order for you' — with a `tool_use` block for `lookup_order`. The harness currently checks whether the response contains any text at all; whenever it does, it treats the turn as finished and returns that text to the customer without executing the tool. What should the harness check instead?
options: Whether the response text is empty — a non-empty reply always signals the turn is complete.
Whether the response's `stop_reason` field equals `tool_use`, and execute every such block regardless of accompanying text.
Whether the response text includes a phrase like 'let me check,' parsed as a natural-language completion cue.
Whether a fixed maximum number of loop iterations has already been reached before running any pending tool call.

whyRight.text: The loop must branch on the structured `stop_reason` field — `tool_use` means execute the pending block regardless of any accompanying acknowledgment text; only `end_turn` means the response is actually finished.

whyWrong.text: Text presence is not the stop signal — Claude can emit acknowledgment text alongside a `tool_use` block in the same response; treating any non-empty text as completion causes exactly this dropped-tool-call bug.
Parsing reply text for a natural-language completion phrase is the documented anti-pattern the exam explicitly rejects in favor of checking the structured `stop_reason` field.
Iteration counts are unrelated to whether Claude still has a pending tool call to run; stopping on a counter instead of `stop_reason` can cut a turn off mid-loop.

questions.stem: In one turn, your agent's response contains three `tool_use` blocks — `get_customer`, `lookup_order`, and `check_warranty_status` — all needed before Claude can continue. The harness executes and appends `tool_result` blocks for the first two, then calls Claude again, planning to supply the third result on a later turn. What is wrong with this approach?
options: Every pending `tool_use` block in that turn needs a matching `tool_result` before the next Claude call; splitting them across turns leaves the batch incomplete.
Nothing — Claude tracks which tool calls are still outstanding across turns using the conversation history alone.
The fix is to raise `max_tokens` so all three tool calls fit inside a single larger response.
The three tools should be consolidated into one composite tool so only a single result needs to be returned.

whyRight.text: The application executes each requested tool and appends a `tool_result` content block for it before Claude continues; leaving one `tool_use` block from the same turn unanswered gives Claude an incomplete context to reason from next.

whyWrong.text: The API is stateless — nothing server-side tracks outstanding tool calls across requests; the messages array the application sends is the only record Claude has of what happened.
`max_tokens` governs response length and produces its own distinct stop reason; it has no bearing on how many `tool_use` blocks a turn contains or whether their results were supplied.
Bundling into a composite tool addresses a different problem — reducing round-trips for tools always called together — not a harness bug that fails to return results for tools it already called.

questions.stem: Your `file_warranty_claim` tool returns a bare `isError: true` whenever a claim is denied because the product is past its warranty window — a written, final policy outcome. The agent treats every denial as an outage: it apologizes for a technical problem and retries, and the ops dashboard now counts these denials as tool failures. How should the tool represent this outcome?
options: Keep returning isError true, but have the tool itself retry automatically up to three times before surfacing anything.
Return isError false with an empty result, since a denied claim is technically a completed lookup.
Add a retryable flag set to true so the agent knows to try the call again with adjusted parameters.
Return `retriable: false` plus a customer-friendly explanation of the policy outcome, so the agent stops retrying and communicates it directly.

whyRight.text: Business-rule errors are a distinct category: `retriable: false` signals that re-invoking cannot change the outcome, and a customer-friendly explanation lets the agent communicate the policy result directly instead of treating it as a failure.

whyWrong.text: Retrying is the correct response only to transient errors like timeouts; a warranty-window denial is a fixed policy outcome that no retry will ever change, so retrying only wastes attempts.
A denial is not an empty result — it is a definite, negative answer the tool determined; masking it as a successful empty lookup hides the actual outcome from the agent's reasoning.
Marking a business-rule denial as retryable is the exact failure mode the exam rejects — it wastes retry attempts on an outcome that can never change regardless of parameters.

questions.stem: Your `reverse_loyalty_redemption` tool permanently claws back redeemed loyalty points and cannot be undone once it runs. Policy requires the agent to show impact details and get explicit confirmation before every reversal. The team is choosing between four designs to guarantee this ordering. Which design makes skipping the preview architecturally impossible, not just discouraged?
options: A single `reverse_loyalty_redemption` tool with a `dry_run: boolean` parameter, defaulting to true.
A system-prompt instruction plus worked examples showing the agent previewing before every reversal.
Two tools: `preview_loyalty_reversal`, returning impact details and a single-use confirmation token, and `execute_loyalty_reversal`, which requires that token.
A server-side timing check that blocks execution if fewer than five seconds have passed since the tool was first called.

whyRight.text: The two-tool token-binding pattern makes the sequence architecturally impossible to skip: no confirmation token exists until a preview call generates one, so execute cannot run first — a code-level guarantee, not a hope.

whyWrong.text: A `dry_run` boolean on a single tool is exactly the design the exam rejects: the agent can call it with `dry_run=false` on the very first attempt, bypassing the preview entirely.
Prompt instructions and few-shot examples are probabilistic — the model may not follow them under load; critical, irreversible sequencing needs a deterministic, code-level guarantee instead.
A server-side timing heuristic is fragile to timing conditions and doesn't actually verify a preview occurred — it can be satisfied by simply waiting, with no preview ever shown.

questions.stem: Your returns-investigation coordinator's prompt is a numbered script: check `lookup_order`, then `check_return_eligibility`, then if eligible call `process_refund`, then done. On a case involving a partial shipment where only some items arrived damaged, the coordinator follows all four steps correctly but never investigates the missing items separately. Which change to the coordinator's prompt is most effective?
options: Rewrite the prompt to state the investigation's goal and quality criteria — full resolution of every issue raised — and let it adapt its steps to what each case reveals.
Add a fifth numbered step specifically checking for missing items after the refund step.
Increase the number of investigation subagents so more cases get dedicated attention.
Add a partial-shipment flag the coordinator checks before starting the fixed sequence.

whyRight.text: Coordinator prompts should specify goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step procedures; a goal-oriented prompt lets the coordinator adapt its investigation to whatever a case reveals, instead of locking into a script that breaks on cases it wasn't written to anticipate.

whyWrong.text: Adding another fixed step deepens the same rigidity that caused the problem — the next case the script doesn't anticipate will surface an identical gap.
More subagents executing the same brittle script does not fix the script; the coordinator's rigid, procedural prompt is the root cause, not a capacity shortage.
A flag for one specific edge case still leaves a fixed, procedural sequence underneath; the underlying problem is the prompt's step-by-step rigidity, not this one missing branch.

questions.stem: Your team ships an `/escalate-case` command so any engineer can type `/escalate-case billing-dispute` to open a pre-formatted escalation with the reason code attached. It must be available to everyone the moment they clone the repository, and the typed reason code must land inside the command's generated note. Where should the command live, and how does it read the typed text?
options: In `~/.claude/commands/`, reading the reason code from an environment variable set before each invocation.
In `.claude/commands/` at the repo root, reading the reason code as `$ARGUMENTS`.
In the personal skills folder, with the reason code hardcoded into the file since commands can't take typed input.
In `~/.claude/skills/escalate-case/`, reading the reason code from the conversation history automatically.

whyRight.text: Project-wide commands live in `.claude/commands/` in the repo, so they're version-controlled and available to everyone on clone; the text typed after the command name is available inside the file as `$ARGUMENTS`.

whyWrong.text: Personal commands in `~/.claude/commands/` aren't shared via version control, so new clones wouldn't get the command; an environment variable also isn't how typed command text is passed in.
Commands and skills can both take the typed text as `$ARGUMENTS`; hardcoding a value defeats the purpose of a reusable command and isn't required.
A personal-scope location isn't shared with the team on clone, and Claude doesn't automatically infer a reason code from conversation history in place of a typed argument.

questions.stem: Your delivery-status subagent's carrier-tracking lookup times out. Instead of reporting the timeout, it silently falls back to a cached status from two days earlier and reports success with no indication the data may be stale. The coordinator presents this to the customer as current. What is the most effective fix?
options: Have the subagent retry the carrier lookup indefinitely until it succeeds, never falling back to cached data.
Have the coordinator re-run the entire case whenever any subagent's tool call is slower than expected.
Have the subagent report the timeout as structured error context — failure type, what was attempted, and that the fallback is stale — instead of masking it as success.
Remove the cached-status fallback entirely so the subagent has nothing to report when a lookup times out.

whyRight.text: A subagent must never catch and silently return success; when it falls back to older data, that must be surfaced as structured context — failure type, what was attempted, and the staleness — so the coordinator can decide how to present it, rather than masking the gap.

whyWrong.text: Retrying indefinitely ignores that a carrier timeout may need a coordinator-level decision — retry, use the fallback with a caveat, or escalate — which the subagent isn't positioned to make alone.
Never terminate the entire workflow for one subagent's failure — re-running the whole case discards other subagents' completed work over a single recoverable timeout.
Removing the fallback doesn't fix the reporting problem; the actual defect is that success was reported without disclosing the fallback, not that a fallback exists at all.

questions.stem: Your team is adding case-escalation ticketing to the support agent's MCP tooling. A well-maintained community MCP server already integrates with your ticketing platform's standard API. An engineer proposes building a custom in-house server instead, arguing it gives the team full control over field mapping. What is the most effective approach?
options: Build the custom server, since any control an engineer might later want justifies the investment upfront.
Use the community server for now, but plan to replace it with a custom one once volume grows.
Run both servers in parallel and let the agent choose whichever responds first for each request.
Use the existing community server for this standard integration, and reserve custom-server effort for workflows unique to the team.

whyRight.text: For standard integrations, prefer existing community MCP servers; build custom servers only for unique, team-specific workflows no existing server covers — building a custom server here reinvents a maintained standard integration.

whyWrong.text: Wanting more control alone doesn't justify reinventing a maintained standard integration; custom-build effort belongs on workflows unique to the team, not a well-covered ticketing API.
There's no documented basis for a volume threshold that should trigger replacing a working community integration with a custom one built for the same standard workflow.
Running duplicate servers for the same capability adds maintenance burden and ambiguity about which result to trust, with no benefit over simply choosing the community server.

questions.stem: Telemetry shows your agent calls `get_customer`, waits a full turn, then calls `fetch_loyalty_tier` with the same customer ID on nearly every loyalty-related case — two round-trips where one would do. An engineer has sketched a combined `get_customer_with_loyalty_tier` tool and asks you to review the design. What should you recommend?
options: Keep the two tools separate and instead prompt the agent to bundle related tool requests into a single turn when both are needed.
Build the combined tool, since it removes a round-trip whenever both pieces of data are needed.
Add a `PreToolUse` hook that automatically calls fetch_loyalty_tier whenever get_customer runs.
Give the agent a tool_choice setting that forces both tools to be named in the same response every time.

whyRight.text: The preferred approach is prompting the agent to bundle related tool requests into one turn, since it can naturally request multiple tools simultaneously — a composite tool hides the composition rather than fixing the sequencing.

whyWrong.text: Building a composite tool is explicitly not the preferred fix here — it hides two distinct operations behind one interface instead of letting the agent request both naturally in one turn.
A hook auto-firing a second tool call on every `get_customer` invocation forces the pairing even for cases that never needed loyalty data, and hooks aren't the documented fix for this pattern.
Forcing both tools into every response over-applies the fix — plenty of cases legitimately need only one of the two, and a blanket tool_choice constraint removes that flexibility.

questions.stem: A customer disputes a $14,000 wire-transfer-linked charge, claiming it was unauthorized. `get_customer` and `lookup_order` both return clean results, but nothing in the transaction history clearly confirms or refutes the claim, and a wrong call either way carries real financial and legal exposure. What should the agent do?
options: Approve the dispute, since a wrongly denied unauthorized-charge claim is the worse outcome for the customer relationship.
Escalate to a human — a wrong decision here carries high-stakes consequences the agent shouldn't resolve alone.
Deny the dispute and cite standard chargeback policy, since no evidence in the record supports the claim.
Ask the customer to resubmit with more documentation before taking any position on the dispute.

whyRight.text: High-stakes ambiguity — where a wrong decision could cause significant harm — is one of the documented escalation triggers; a large disputed charge with genuinely unclear evidence is exactly this case, not one the agent should resolve unilaterally.

whyWrong.text: Approving without evidence isn't a policy-authorized action; the agent must not invent a resolution favoring one side when the case is genuinely ambiguous and high-stakes.
Denying based on the absence of confirming evidence overstates what an unclear record actually shows, and risks a wrong call on a high-exposure case the agent isn't positioned to close out alone.
Requesting more documentation delays without resolving the actual decision point — the ambiguity here isn't a missing-information gap the customer can fill, it's a high-stakes judgment call.

questions.stem: After an expensive investigation into a customer's disputed multi-order billing history, the team wants to evaluate two candidate resolutions — a partial refund versus a full account credit — starting from that same completed investigation, without either evaluation's reasoning influencing the other. What is the most effective way to continue?
options: Resume the investigation session and evaluate both resolutions in it, one after the other.
Start two brand-new sessions and have each independently redo the full billing investigation.
Use `fork_session` to branch two independent sessions from the completed investigation's shared baseline.
Resume the session and ask it to weigh both resolutions together in a single combined recommendation.

whyRight.text: `fork_session` creates branches that inherit context up to the branch point, then diverge independently — exactly what's needed to compare two candidate resolutions from one shared, expensive baseline without either contaminating the other.

whyWrong.text: Evaluating both resolutions sequentially in the same resumed session lets the second evaluation's reasoning be biased by the first's conclusions — the opposite of an independent comparison.
Two brand-new sessions would each have to redo the expensive investigation from scratch, wasting the work already completed and shared by both candidate resolutions.
A single combined recommendation isn't an independent comparison of the two options — it collapses exactly the separation `fork_session` exists to preserve.

questions.stem: Before an escalation summary reaches a human agent, your team routes it through a second Claude Code instance that has no access to the first, drafting instance's reasoning trace, and asks it to independently flag any missing context or unsupported claims before the handoff goes out. Which named architecture pattern does this design exemplify?
options: Evaluator-optimizer — a generator produces the draft, and an independent critic reviews it separately.
Coverage annotation — the output is marked showing which conclusions are well-supported versus where gaps exist.
Structured error propagation — failures are reported with type, attempted action, and partial results.
Context isolation — a subagent receives only what the coordinator explicitly chooses to pass it.

whyRight.text: Evaluator-optimizer names exactly this two-stage design: a generator produces the draft, and an independent critic or reviewer instance evaluates it separately, mirroring human peer review without the drafting instance's confirmation bias.

whyWrong.text: Coverage annotation describes marking which synthesis conclusions are well-supported versus data-gapped, not a second independent instance reviewing a completed draft for missed context.
Structured error propagation describes how a failing subagent reports failure type, attempted parameters, and partial results — this scenario has no failure being reported.
Context isolation describes what a subagent receives from the coordinator, not a second reviewing instance independently evaluating a completed draft afterward.

questions.stem: Your support agent already extracts precise transactional facts — order ID, agreed credit amount, promised delivery date — into a persistent case-facts block included in every prompt, outside the summarized conversation history. An engineer proposes replacing it with a vector-database retrieval system 'to make fact recall more robust.' How should the team evaluate this proposal?
options: Adopt it — semantic retrieval is always a stronger foundation for precise numeric recall than a structured block.
Adopt it, but keep the case-facts block too, so both mechanisms independently store the same figures.
Reject it, and instead raise the summarization threshold so the existing history compresses less often.
Reject it — the case-facts block already solves session-level precision; external retrieval infrastructure is overkill for facts that fit in a single persistent block.

whyRight.text: The persistent case-facts block already survives summarization by living outside compressed history; adding external storage and retrieval is unneeded infrastructure for facts that comfortably fit in one small, always-included block — overkill for session-level precision.

whyWrong.text: Semantic retrieval is suited to recalling specific exchanges across months of history, not to a handful of precise transactional figures a case-facts block already carries reliably in every prompt.
Running both mechanisms for the same figures adds complexity and a second source of truth to keep in sync, with no accuracy gain the case-facts block doesn't already provide.

Raising the summarization threshold only delays compression — the facts still eventually pass into summarized history and lose precision, and it doesn't address a proposal for a block that already avoids that failure mode.

questions.stem: A customer calls in and gives only a phone number to identify themselves. The `get_customer` tool returns three separate accounts sharing that number, since the number is registered to a shared family plan. The agent must proceed on the correct one before discussing any order or billing detail. What should it do?
options: Select the account with the most recent order activity, since that's the account most likely calling in now.
Ask the customer for an additional identifier, such as an email address or order number, to confirm the right account.
Select the first account the tool returns and proceed, correcting course later if the customer objects.
Escalate to a human immediately, since multiple accounts sharing one phone number can't be resolved by the agent.

whyRight.text: When a lookup returns several matching records, the agent must request additional identifiers — email, order number, another detail — never pick a match by heuristic; this resolves the ambiguity directly.

whyWrong.text: Picking the account with the most recent activity is exactly the heuristic-selection pattern the exam rejects — it risks acting on the wrong family member's account and discussing the wrong order or billing detail.
Selecting the first result is arbitrary and carries the same misidentification risk as picking by recency; nothing about tool result order indicates which account is actually calling.
Escalating is unnecessary here — the ambiguity is directly resolvable by asking for one more identifier, without involving a human.

questions.stem: Your agent auto-closes cases whenever its per-field confidence on the resolution details is high, and human reviewers only ever look at the low-confidence cases flagged for review. Months later, a reviewer stumbles onto a systematic error affecting a class of auto-closed cases that had never been sampled. What should the oversight design add?
options: Lower the confidence threshold so more cases route to human review by default.
A second, independent confidence score computed by the same model on the same resolution.
Regular stratified random sampling of the high-confidence, auto-closed stream, not only the flagged low-confidence cases.
A quarterly survey asking customers whether their auto-closed case felt correctly resolved.

whyRight.text: Even high-confidence outputs need regular, stratified auditing — sampling only the flagged low-confidence stream leaves the automated high-confidence path completely unmeasured, letting a novel, systematic error pattern compound undetected exactly as happened here.

whyWrong.text: Lowering the threshold routes more cases to review generally, but doesn't add the stratified auditing of the high-confidence stream needed to catch a systematic error already living inside cases the model is confident about.

A second score from the same model on the same resolution isn't independent, ground-truth-based measurement — self-reported confidence is exactly what needs calibration and auditing against a validation source, not more of itself.

Customer sentiment about whether a case 'felt' correctly resolved is not the same as verified resolution accuracy and isn't the documented oversight mechanism for catching systematic errors in the automated stream.

questions.stem: A platform team's onboarding agent runs a code-review subagent and a test-generation subagent under one coordinator. To save a round trip, an engineer proposes letting the two subagents message each other directly with extra test scenarios, skipping the coordinator. What is the strongest reason to keep this routed through the coordinator?
options: The coordinator keeps full visibility into every inter-agent request and can apply uniform error handling and information control — direct peer messaging removes that centralized oversight.
Peer-to-peer messaging distributes error handling across subagents, which reduces the coordinator's workload and scales better as the agent roster grows.
Coordinator mediation only matters once three or more subagents run in parallel; two subagents exchanging one message don't need it.
Routing through the coordinator only pays off at larger scale, so bypassing it for a single exchange is a reasonable optimization.

whyRight.text: Hub-and-spoke keeps the coordinator as the single point of visibility, giving it centralized, uniform error handling and control over what context each subagent receives — properties that direct subagent-to-subagent messaging removes.

whyWrong.text: The corpus treats centralized error handling as the benefit of the hub-and-spoke pattern, not something a coordinator sheds by delegating; decentralized handling is the failure mode, not an efficiency gain.
The pattern's correctness doesn't hinge on how many subagents are involved or whether calls are parallel — the coordinator mediates every inter-agent exchange regardless of scale.
Hub-and-spoke is the correct architecture independent of scale; treating coordinator mediation as overhead to shed for a single exchange misreads why the pattern exists.

questions.stem: After a schema change, an automation must regenerate a config file where nearly every line differs from the previous version. The current script issues a separate targeted-replacement call per changed line, and several calls fail because the old text no longer appears verbatim. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Keep retrying the same targeted-replacement call with a shorter anchor string, hoping a shorter match is less likely to collide.
Read the file's current contents, generate the updated version, and write it back in one pass — appropriate when most of the content is changing, not a small portion.
Switch to a shell-based find-and-replace command so the substitution no longer depends on matching existing text.
Enumerate matching file paths first, then keep using the same targeted-replacement call, since that confirms the file's identity beforehand.

whyRight.text: When most of a file's content is changing, a unique-anchor targeted replacement isn't the right tool at all — reading the file, generating the new version, and writing it back is the sanctioned approach for wholesale changes.

whyWrong.text: Shorter anchor strings are more likely to match multiple locations, not fewer — this makes the ambiguity worse, and it doesn't address the deeper issue that most of the file is changing anyway.

A shell-based find-and-replace bypasses the tool built for reliable file modification; the sanctioned fallback for this case is reading and rewriting the file, not routing around it with a shell command.
Enumerating file paths locates which file to change, but it does nothing about a targeted-replacement call failing because the anchor text isn't unique or the change is too broad for that mechanism.

questions.stem: A monorepo's infra/terraform/ directory requires every modified file to carry a change-justification comment — a rule that applies nowhere else in the repository, regardless of which service's code sits alongside it. Where should this rule live so it loads automatically only when Terraform files are touched, without bloating every other session?
options: In root CLAUDE.md under a Terraform heading, trusting the model to apply it only when Terraform files are present.
As a Skill invoked explicitly before committing Terraform changes, so engineers have to remember to run it manually.
In `.claude/rules/terraform.md` with frontmatter scoping it to `infra/terraform/**`, so it loads automatically only for matching files.
In a separate `CLAUDE.md` placed inside `infra/terraform/`, since directory-level files apply only within that subdirectory.

whyRight.text: Path-scoped rules with YAML frontmatter glob patterns load automatically only when Claude is working on matching files, keeping the Terraform-specific requirement out of every other session.

whyWrong.text: A CLAUDE.md heading loads into every session regardless of which files are being touched and relies on the model inferring when to apply it, rather than deterministic path matching.
A Skill is workflow-scoped and invoked on demand — it depends on the engineer remembering to run it, which doesn't guarantee the rule applies on every Terraform edit.

Scattering a separate CLAUDE.md per directory is the documented weaker alternative to rules/ glob patterns, especially awkward once the scoped convention needs to apply more precisely than a whole subdirectory.

questions.stem: The `resolve_module_owner` tool description reads only: 'Returns the current owner of a module.' It works only for actively maintained modules — for archived ones it returns stale data with no warning, and engineers now cite that output as authoritative. What is the most effective fix?
options: Rename the tool to a more specific name without changing its description, since a clearer name alone resolves the ambiguity.
Leave the description as-is and add a pre-routing classifier that filters out archived modules before the call is made.
Add a `dry_run` parameter so engineers can preview whether a module is archived before trusting the result.
Expand the description to state explicitly that results are unreliable for archived or deprecated modules, so the agent recognizes the boundary case.

whyRight.text: A good tool description states what a tool does, what input it needs, and explicitly names its boundary cases — where it should NOT be trusted — which is exactly the gap here.

whyWrong.text: A clearer name alone doesn't communicate the boundary case; the exam principle is that descriptions, not names, are the primary lever the model reasons from.
Adding a classifier is infrastructure layered on top of an under-specified description — the corpus's rule is to fix the description first, not compensate for it with a new component.
A `dry_run` parameter solves a different problem — guaranteeing a mandatory preview before an action — not a description that fails to flag when a result is unreliable.

questions.stem: The automation's `generate_release_notes` tool must run only after `tag_release` finishes, since notes reference the new tag. This ordering exists only as a step in the system prompt. When a slow CI run delayed `tag_release`, the agent invoked `generate_release_notes` first, producing notes citing a tag that didn't exist yet. What change most reliably prevents this?
options: Reorder the system prompt so the tag-creation step is described before the release-notes step, making the sequence read unambiguously.
Add a programmatic precondition that blocks `generate_release_notes` from running until `tag_release` has returned a completed tag identifier.
Add a few-shot example showing the correct call order, so the agent has a concrete pattern to imitate.
Increase the delay between the two calls so tag creation has more time to finish first.

whyRight.text: A programmatic precondition makes the dependency architecturally enforced — the second tool literally cannot run without the first completing — where a prompt-only rule remains probabilistic.

whyWrong.text: Reordering prose in the system prompt is still a prompt instruction; the model can still deviate from it under load or ambiguity, since nothing enforces the order in code.
Few-shot examples make correct behavior more likely, not guaranteed — for a consistency-critical ordering, that's the same probabilistic reliability the corpus warns against.
A fixed delay is a timing heuristic that assumes a particular latency; it's fragile to slow runs and doesn't actually verify the first step completed.

questions.stem: The `check_deprecated_packages` audit tool returns an empty result list both when a repository genuinely has zero deprecated packages, and when its backend vulnerability index is unreachable — the same signal either way. Engineers now can't tell a clean audit from one that silently didn't run. What should the tool's response distinguish?
options: Return a genuine empty result set only for a real zero-findings audit, and a distinct access-failure signal when the index couldn't be reached — never collapse the two into the same empty response.
Keep returning an empty list for both cases, since the automation only needs to know whether remediation is required, not why the list came back empty.
Flag every empty result as a failure to be safe, so engineers double-check even genuinely clean audits before trusting them.
Automatically retry once on any empty result before reporting, in case the first response was a transient fluke.

whyRight.text: An empty result is a successful, informative answer — zero deprecated packages — and must be distinguishable from a query that couldn't run at all; conflating the two in either direction corrupts what the agent reports downstream.

whyWrong.text: Collapsing both cases into the same empty response means the automation can silently report "clean" when the audit never actually ran — exactly the corrupted decision-making the corpus warns an ambiguous empty signal causes.
Flagging every empty result as a failure treats a valid, successful zero-findings answer as an error, causing the agent to needlessly re-work or escalate audits that already succeeded.
A blind retry does nothing to distinguish the two cases going forward — a genuine zero-findings audit gets retried for no reason, and an unreachable index likely fails the same way again.

questions.stem: An engineer assumes the shared `.claude/skills/commit/SKILL.md` always wins over any personal skill with the same name, reasoning project config should win since it's what the team agreed on. After the team updates the shared skill's checks, the engineer's `/commit` behavior doesn't change at all. What is going on?
options: Rename personal experiments to a different command instead, so a same-named override can never occur in the first place.
Shared skills can't be overridden by personal configuration at all — only standalone slash commands support personal overrides.
The engineer is right that project configuration always wins; the shared update should have applied, so this must be a caching bug.
Personal skills override project skills sharing the same name — the engineer's command almost certainly resolves to their own `~/.claude/skills/commit/SKILL.md`.

whyRight.text: Personal skills at `~/.claude/skills/` override project skills of the same name — the engineer's shared-skill update never had a chance to matter because their own personal override is what actually runs.

whyWrong.text: Renaming to a different command avoids future collisions but doesn't explain the current behavior, and it also loses the familiar `/commit` name for that engineer.
Commands and skills are unified in current Claude Code — the same-name override rule applies to both, not just to commands.
This inverts the actual precedence rule — project configuration does not automatically win; a personal skill of the same name takes precedence, which is exactly what's masking the update.

questions.stem: A mapping subagent and a dependency-audit subagent independently report the same module's line count — 2,340 and 2,510 — because they ran against different commits. Both numbers reach the report-writing subagent as plain sentences, with no timestamp or commit reference attached, and it silently keeps the audit subagent's figure. What should change?
options: Have the report-writing subagent always prefer whichever figure is higher, treating the larger number as the safer estimate to report.
Instruct the report-writing subagent in its prompt to double-check figures against each other before writing them down.

Require each subagent's output to carry structured metadata, including which commit each figure was measured against, so the report-writing subagent can preserve and attribute both figures instead of silently picking one.
Have the report-writing subagent re-run its own line-count check to settle which figure is correct before writing the report.

whyRight.text: Structured metadata carrying each figure's source commit lets the report-writing subagent preserve and attribute both values instead of merging them into a single unsourced number — the corpus's explicit rule for conflicting statistics.

whyWrong.text: Picking whichever number is larger is an arbitrary rule with no connection to which figure is actually correct for the report's intended commit — it doesn't resolve the underlying attribution loss.
A prompt instruction to double-check is probabilistic and still doesn't give the subagent the structured metadata needed to actually reconcile or attribute the two figures.

Having the report-writing subagent re-run the line-count check duplicates work already done by a specialized subagent and breaks the separation of responsibilities between mapping/audit and reporting roles.

questions.stem: Three internal MCP tools return timestamps in different formats: Unix epoch from one, ISO 8601 from another, a locale-formatted string from a third. None of these tools are ones the team controls. Downstream reporting has started mis-ordering build history because of the mismatch. What is the most effective fix?
options: Add a `PostToolUse` hook that intercepts each tool's output and normalizes all timestamps to one format before results reach the agent's context.
Document each tool's timestamp format in the system prompt so the agent converts them consistently when writing the report.
Create a dedicated normalization tool the agent calls after every retrieval to convert the value.
Fork each of the three tools' source code and patch them to emit one consistent format.

whyRight.text: A `PostToolUse` hook intercepts and normalizes output centrally and deterministically, working even for third-party tools the team cannot modify — the corpus's primary use case for this hook.

whyWrong.text: Documenting formats in the system prompt relies on the LLM correctly interpreting and converting three different formats every time, which is probabilistic, not guaranteed.
A tool the agent must remember to call after every retrieval adds an extra LLM call and depends on the agent reliably invoking it — hooks avoid that overhead entirely.
Patching source code you don't control creates fragmented, unmaintainable forks of tools the team doesn't own — exactly the alternative the corpus rejects.

questions.stem: A dependency-scanning subagent audits every service's lockfile for outdated packages. One lockfile fails to parse after a tooling upgrade changed its schema, so the subagent silently substitutes last week's cached scan for that service instead of failing. The report lists every service's findings with identical confidence, stale data included. What should the output do instead?
options: Drop the affected service from the report entirely, since a stale substitution is worse than no data at all.
Complete the report using available data, but annotate the substituted service's findings as based on stale, pre-upgrade data, flagging the confidence difference.
Re-run the entire audit for every service once the parser is fixed, and hold the whole report until then.
Return an error for the whole audit run, since one service's data cannot be verified as current.

whyRight.text: Graceful degradation means completing the report from available data while explicitly annotating which parts rest on lower-confidence or stale input, propagating the uncertainty instead of hiding it.

whyWrong.text: Dropping the service discards recoverable value — the stale data is still informative once flagged, and omission throws away information the corpus says should be annotated, not deleted.
Holding the entire report hostage to one recoverable parsing gap blocks a deliverable that's otherwise complete and correct for every other service.
Returning an error for the whole run treats a partial, still-usable result as a total failure — the corpus's principle is to complete and annotate, not abort.

questions.stem: An engineer unfamiliar with the team's job queue asks Claude Code to add deduplication so a job never runs twice concurrently. The first version misses cross-instance duplication, the second misses a dedup key that changes mid-retry, the third leaves stale locks after a crash — a different gap each time. What is the most effective next step?
options: Keep iterating on the current implementation, addressing each newly discovered gap as it surfaces.
Ask Claude Code to write an exhaustive design document covering every conceivable distributed-systems edge case before any code is written.
Switch to generating the deduplication logic with a larger, more capable model, since the current model keeps missing requirements.
Restart the task and have Claude Code interview the engineer first — asking about cross-instance behavior, retry key-changes, and crash recovery — before generating any implementation.

whyRight.text: The interview pattern front-loads exactly the domain-specific questions — cross-instance behavior, key changes, crash recovery — that three separate generation attempts each discovered the hard way, replacing several correction cycles with one clarifying turn.

whyWrong.text: Continuing to patch one newly discovered gap at a time is the slow, reactive pattern the corpus contrasts against front-loaded clarification — each fix risks missing the next gap.
An exhaustive upfront design document isn't the interview pattern — it substitutes broad, generic coverage for a few targeted questions specific to this task's actual unknowns.
The repeated misses trace to unsurfaced requirements, not generation quality — a larger model would face the same unspecified requirements and likely miss them too.

questions.stem: The build-automation subagent has accumulated 18 tools across three MCP servers plus all six built-ins, added as new needs arose. It frequently calls the wrong one among near-duplicate options, even after every description was rewritten to be clearer. What is the most effective next step?
options: Restrict the subagent's tool set to the handful actually relevant to its role, reducing what it must discriminate between each turn.
Keep all 18 tools, since removing any could be useful, and add a `tool_choice` pre-filter that narrows the candidate set each turn.
Leave the tool set as-is; the recent description rewrite just needs more time to take effect.
Give every other subagent the same 18-tool set too, so tool access stays consistent across the team's automations.

whyRight.text: Reducing the tool count to the 4-5 actually relevant to the role shrinks the decision space the model must discriminate across on every turn — the corpus's documented fix once description quality alone hasn't resolved misrouting.

whyWrong.text: A pre-filtering classifier is infrastructure added on top of an oversized tool set rather than reducing the set itself — the corpus treats tool count as the root cause here, not a symptom to route around.
The scenario states descriptions were already rewritten and misrouting persisted — the bottleneck is tool count, not description clarity needing more time.
Broadening every subagent's tool set to match spreads the same reliability problem to peers that currently select correctly with a smaller, role-scoped set.

questions.stem: The boilerplate-generation subagent scaffolds new module files from a template — nothing else. Its AgentDefinition includes shell access, added at design time on the reasoning that scaffolding might someday need a shell command. It has since started running git history-rewriting commands on branches other subagents are also working on. What is the most effective fix?
options: Add a system-prompt instruction telling the subagent to only use its shell access for scaffolding commands, never git history operations.
Leave shell access in place, since removing it would block any legitimate command scaffolding might someday need.
Remove `Bash` from the subagent's allowed tools and give it only `Write` and `Edit`, since scaffolding never actually required a shell command.
Add a `PreToolUse` hook that blocks only the specific history-rewriting commands, leaving shell access otherwise available.

whyRight.text: Removing the unneeded shell access entirely closes the capability at the interface level — a scaffolding role that only ever needs to write files has no legitimate use for a shell tool in the first place.

whyWrong.text: A prompt instruction restricting how a tool is used is probabilistic — it doesn't remove the capability, so the subagent can still deviate from it.
Keeping broad access 'in case it's needed someday' is exactly the anti-pattern least-privilege design rejects — scope to what the role actually requires now.

Blocking only the two specific commands seen so far leaves the underlying broad shell access in place for whatever misuse comes next — the fix belongs at the tool-scope level, not a growing blocklist.

questions.stem: Designing the build-automation agent's MCP server, the team must expose three things: `trigger_rebuild` and `invalidate_cache`, actions the agent performs; a build-configuration reference the agent should only ever read, never edit; and a reusable postmortem template the agent fills in after a failed build. Which MCP primitive should carry each?
options: Expose all three as tools, since a single uniform interface is simpler for the agent to reason about than mixing primitive types.
Expose the rebuild/cache actions as tools, the build-configuration reference as a resource, and the postmortem template as a prompt.
Expose the actions as resources so their effects stay auditable, and the configuration reference and template as tools.
Expose the actions as tools, the configuration reference as a prompt, and the postmortem template as a resource.

whyRight.text: The three MCP primitives map by capability: tools are actions Claude calls, resources are read-only data Claude can access, and prompts are pre-built reusable templates — matching the rebuild/cache actions, the read-only config reference, and the fill-in-the-blank postmortem template exactly.

whyWrong.text: Forcing the read-only reference and the reusable template into the tools primitive discards the protocol's distinction between an action Claude invokes and data or a template it merely consumes.

Resources are read-only by design and cannot represent actions like triggering a rebuild or invalidating a cache — auditability is a property of logging the action, not of misclassifying it as a resource.
This swaps the reference and the template's roles: a static reference document the agent reads is a resource, not a prompt, and a reusable fill-in template is a prompt, not a resource.

questions.stem: Code generation and code review run as two separate Claude Code sessions with no shared conversation history — independent on paper. Both, however, were configured with the same few-shot example set, which happens to omit a common null-input edge case. The reviewer approves a generated function that mishandles exactly that case. What is the most effective fix?
options: Give the reviewer session extended thinking so it reasons more carefully before approving.
Add a self-review instruction to the generator's own prompt asking it to double-check edge cases before finishing.
Merge the two sessions into one, since running them separately clearly isn't preventing missed edge cases anyway.
Give the reviewer session a different, independently curated example set that includes edge cases the generator's set omits, so its independence isn't undermined by sharing the same blind spot.

whyRight.text: True independence requires the reviewer's inputs, not just its conversation history, to differ from the generator's — sharing the same example set reproduces the same blind spot even without any shared session or transcript.

whyWrong.text: Extended thinking makes the reviewer reason longer over the same inputs; it doesn't introduce the missing null-input example the shared set never included.
A self-review instruction added to the generator's own prompt keeps the check inside the same instance and the same reasoning that produced the bug — the opposite of independent review.
Merging the two sessions removes even the nominal separation that exists today, which moves further from independent review, not toward a fix.

questions.stem: Your CI coordinator runs three independent analysis subagents on every PR — correctness, style, and dependency-risk — each spawned via a separate `Task` call. Today the coordinator emits one `Task` call, waits for its subagent to finish, then emits the next `Task` call in a following response, tripling wall-clock time versus running all three together. What is the most effective fix?
options: Emit all three `Task` calls together in a single coordinator response so the subagents run in parallel, rather than spreading them across separate turns.
Increase the CI runner's parallelism setting so multiple pipeline jobs can execute at once, leaving the coordinator's own sequential calling pattern unchanged.
Merge the three subagents into one combined agent that performs correctness, style, and dependency-risk checks itself, avoiding delegation entirely.
Keep the three sequential Task calls but reduce each subagent's scope so individual calls complete faster.

whyRight.text: Multiple Task calls issued together in one coordinator response execute in parallel; spreading them across separate responses forces them to run sequentially, exactly the tripled wall-clock time observed here.

whyWrong.text: Runner-level parallelism affects other CI jobs, not this coordinator's own sequential Task-calling pattern — the fix has to change how and when the Task calls are emitted.
Merging distinct specialist subagents into one loses the benefit of parallel, independently-scoped delegation and doesn't address the actual sequencing defect.
Shrinking each subagent's scope reduces per-call latency, but the three calls are still emitted across separate turns, so they still run one after another.

questions.stem: After an incident where a `/apply-autofix` skill's Bash access let it run an unintended shell script mid-fix, the team is scoping a new `/format-pr` skill that should only ever read and edit files during PR formatting cleanup — never execute shell commands. Which SKILL.md frontmatter change most directly enforces this?
options: Add a `context: fork` entry so the skill's actions run in an isolated subagent, away from the main session.
Set `allowed-tools: [Read, Edit]` in the skill's frontmatter so its execution is scoped to those two tools.
Add a hint describing the expected input so engineers invoke the skill correctly.
Move the skill to the older commands-style location for a stricter execution model.

whyRight.text: `allowed-tools` in SKILL.md frontmatter is the mechanism for scoping which tools a skill may use during execution — restricting it to `[Read, Edit]` keeps `/format-pr` from ever reaching Bash.

whyWrong.text: `context: fork` isolates a skill's output/context from the main session; it does not restrict which tools the skill is permitted to call.
`argument-hint` only affects what's displayed when invoking the command — it has no effect on tool access.
`.claude/commands/` and `.claude/skills/` are functionally unified naming locations for the same `/name` mechanism; moving between them doesn't add a tool-scoping restriction.

questions.stem: A new CI step must run Claude Code fully unattended to review each pull request; no one is available to answer interactive prompts. An engineer, unfamiliar with the CLI, sets `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` in the pipeline's environment config, expecting it to suppress interactive prompts. The step still hangs waiting for input on every run. What actually fixes this?
options: Increase the CI runner's timeout so the step has more time to wait for `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` to take effect.
Add `--batch` to the invocation alongside the existing environment variable.
Invoke Claude Code with `-p` (or `--print`), which processes the prompt, prints to stdout, and exits without waiting for interactive input.
Pipe `stdin < /dev/null` into the invocation while leaving everything else unchanged.

whyRight.text: `-p`/`--print` is the documented flag for non-interactive Claude Code — it processes the prompt, prints the result, and exits; without it, Claude Code waits for interactive input and a pipeline hangs.

whyWrong.text: `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` is not a real Claude Code setting — no amount of waiting makes a nonexistent environment variable take effect.
`--batch` is not a documented Claude Code flag.
Redirecting stdin from `/dev/null` is an undocumented Unix workaround, not the sanctioned approach — `-p` is.

questions.stem: Your CI pipeline's merge gate calls `claude -p` and needs a single verdict object — a `pass_fail` flag plus a list of blocking file paths — to decide whether the queue unblocks a PR. Prose responses vary in wording enough that the gate script's parser fails on roughly one run in twenty. Which configuration most reliably guarantees parseable output?
options: Add a line to CLAUDE.md instructing Claude to always respond with the verdict object in JSON.
Add a formatting instruction directly in the prompt describing the exact JSON shape expected.
Increase `max_tokens` so the response always has enough room to include a complete JSON block.
Invoke with `--output-format json` and `--json-schema` to enforce the verdict object's exact schema.

whyRight.text: `--output-format json` together with `--json-schema` forces schema-conformant JSON the gate script can reliably parse — a guarantee prompt-based or CLAUDE.md-based instructions can't provide.

whyWrong.text: A CLAUDE.md instruction to respond in JSON is not enforced — the model can still return prose, exactly the intermittent failure already being seen.
A prompt-level formatting instruction is compliance the model may or may not follow on any given run — it doesn't remove the underlying variability.
A token-budget increase addresses truncation, not format compliance — the parser is failing on wording variance, not on cut-off responses.

questions.stem: Finance asks your team to move the CI pipeline's pre-merge review — the check a PR cannot merge without, while the author waits on the result — onto the Message Batches API to capture its 50% cost discount. What should the team do?
options: Keep it synchronous — the Batches API has no latency SLA and can take up to 24 hours, unacceptable for a check the author is actively blocked on.
Move it to batch; the 50% savings apply regardless of what kind of workload it is.
Move it to batch, then poll frequently, since testing shows batches usually return within an hour.
Split the review into two parallel batch requests to halve the worst-case latency.

whyRight.text: Batch is for non-blocking, latency-tolerant work; a pre-merge check the author is waiting on must match its API to the latency requirement and stay synchronous, since batch carries no latency SLA.

whyWrong.text: Cost savings don't override the latency mismatch — a blocking check cannot tolerate an up-to-24-hour, no-SLA response time regardless of discount.
Typical fast turnaround in testing doesn't remove the lack of an SLA — the one run that takes the full 24 hours defeats the point of a pre-merge gate.
Splitting into more batch requests doesn't change the API's own processing-window guarantee — each request still carries the same no-SLA risk.

questions.stem: Your CI pipeline's CLAUDE.md holds three kinds of guidance: formatting conventions every review must follow, a security-review checklist invoked only during periodic audits, and a stricter validation rule that should apply automatically whenever Claude Code touches files under `payments/`. An engineer proposes bundling the checklist and the payments rule into one new Skill, leaving only formatting in CLAUDE.md. How should the team evaluate this?
options: Approve the proposal — bundling both non-universal items into one Skill is a reasonable consolidation.

Split three ways instead: keep formatting in CLAUDE.md, move the security checklist to a Skill invoked on demand, and move the `payments/` rule to `.claude/rules/` with a path glob so it loads automatically.
Move all three, including the universal formatting conventions, into the same new Skill.
Reject the proposal and leave all three exactly where they are in CLAUDE.md.

whyRight.text: Universal, always-relevant content stays in CLAUDE.md; workflow-specific guidance invoked on demand (the security checklist) belongs in a Skill; conventions that should load automatically based on file location (the `payments/` rule) belong in `.claude/rules/` with a glob — a Skill only loads on explicit invocation, so it can't provide that automatic path-triggered behavior.

whyWrong.text: The `payments/` rule needs to load automatically whenever matching files are touched; a Skill only runs when explicitly invoked, so bundling it in loses that automatic trigger.
Moving the universal formatting conventions into a Skill means they no longer load by default — every session would need an explicit invocation to get baseline conventions.
Leaving all three in CLAUDE.md loads the security checklist and the payments-specific rule into every session regardless of relevance — the exact 'wall of rules' problem this section addresses.

questions.stem: A named Claude Code session spent a full day mapping how the CI pipeline's retry-and-backoff logic works, ahead of a planned refactor. Before the team picks the work back up, an unrelated migration this week rewrote that retry logic entirely. What is the most effective way to continue?
options: `--resume` the named session and continue directly from where the mapping left off.
`fork_session` from the named session to branch into the refactor work.
Start a fresh session, briefed with a short summary of the prior mapping's key findings, rather than resuming the named session.
Resume the named session and run a context-compaction pass so it re-reads the current state of the retry logic.

whyRight.text: When tool results are stale — here, the entire retry-and-backoff logic the session mapped no longer describes the actual code — starting fresh with a short summary of prior findings beats resuming a session anchored to now-incorrect tool results.

whyWrong.text: Resuming carries forward the session's stale tool results from before the migration rewrote the retry logic — the session doesn't know its own findings are now wrong.

`fork_session` inherits the same context up to the branch point, so a fork of this session still starts from the same stale mapping; it's for comparing two approaches from a shared valid baseline, not for recovering from staleness.
`/compact` compresses existing context — it doesn't re-execute any exploration or refresh stale tool results with current file contents.

questions.stem: Your CI pipeline's test-generation step defines a separate test-writing tool per language — `write_python_test`, `write_js_test`, `write_go_test` — each shaped to that framework's assertion style. A PR's diff includes template files whose eventual language isn't determined by file extension alone, and the step must still emit one schema-valid test definition per changed file, never a prose explanation. Which `tool_choice` configuration is most effective?
options: `{"type": "tool", "name": "write_python_test"}`, forcing the Python tool on every call.
`{"type": "auto"}`, letting the model decide whether to call a tool or explain in text.
Leave `tool_choice` at its default and add a prompt instruction: 'always call the matching test-writing tool for this file's language.'
`{"type": "any"}`, requiring the model to call some test-writing tool while letting it pick the one that fits the file's actual language.

whyRight.text: `{"type": "any"}` guarantees a tool call happens on every file — always structured output — while still letting the model choose whichever language-specific tool actually fits, exactly the case where the correct type isn't known ahead of time.

whyWrong.text: Forcing `write_python_test` specifically guarantees structure only for Python files — it produces a wrong or failing call for every JS or Go file in the diff.
`{"type": "auto"}` leaves the model free to explain in prose instead of calling any tool — no structure guarantee at all.
A prompt instruction to 'always call the matching tool' is probabilistic compliance, not a guarantee — the same class of failure `tool_choice` exists to eliminate.

questions.stem: The team adds few-shot examples teaching the review bot which findings should block a merge outright versus post as a non-blocking comment. The first draft has fifteen examples: ten obvious blocking cases (a hardcoded credential) and five obvious non-blocking ones (a naming nit). The bot still guesses inconsistently on genuinely borderline cases — a caught-but-unhandled edge case, a deprecated-but-functional call. What is the most effective revision?
options: Replace the set with 4-6 examples targeted specifically at the genuinely ambiguous cases, each with a rationale for the call made.
Add ten more obvious blocking examples so the ratio of blocking to non-blocking examples better reflects real traffic.
Replace the examples with a more detailed written rule distinguishing blocking from non-blocking findings.
Have the bot self-rate its confidence in each finding and auto-block anything below a fixed threshold.

whyRight.text: Few-shot examples are most effective when targeted at exactly the ambiguous cases where the model gets it wrong — a handful of well-chosen borderline examples outperforms many examples of clear-cut cases the model already handles correctly.

whyWrong.text: More clear-cut examples don't teach the boundary — the bot is already correct on obvious cases; the failure is specifically on borderline ones.
Written instructions are already what's failing to draw a consistent boundary; more prose doesn't fix what examples are better suited to demonstrate.
Model self-rated confidence is a poorly-calibrated proxy for actual difficulty — a confidently-wrong call on a borderline case is exactly the failure mode being reported.

questions.stem: An engineer wants the review bot to respond in a fixed JSON-only format, with no prose preamble, for the life of the CI run. They set an environment variable, RESPONSE_FORMAT=json, in the pipeline's runner config, expecting the harness to relay it to Claude before each call. Responses keep mixing in prose anyway. Where should this constraint actually be defined?
options: In the first user message of each run, since that's where the model reads its immediate instructions.
In the system prompt, where persistent behavioral and response-format constraints belong for the entire conversation.
In the first assistant message, prefilled to demonstrate the expected JSON-only style.
The environment variable approach is correct — the harness just needs to be fixed to actually forward it.

whyRight.text: The system prompt is the correct location for persistent behavioral rules and response-format requirements that should hold for an entire conversation.

whyWrong.text: A constraint stated only in the first user message can lose authority as later messages accumulate — it's not the durable, per-request-included instruction the system prompt provides.
A prefilled first assistant message the model 'said' itself doesn't bind later responses — the model can still deviate from its own earlier statement.
Environment variables have no effect on model behavior at all — the API has no mechanism to read pipeline env vars into a request; the constraint has to be an actual message field.

questions.stem: Mid-run, a critical CVE advisory is published for a dependency the pipeline is currently reviewing a PR against. The team wants the review bot's very next response, still in the same run, to factor in this new advisory without waiting for the pipeline's next full invocation. What is the most effective way to inject this?
options: Rewrite the system prompt to mention the new advisory, then continue the run.
Send a separate, synthetic user-role message announcing the advisory before the next real turn.
Wait for the next scheduled pipeline invocation, when the advisory can be included in the initial prompt.
Prefix the advisory details onto the next user message the bot processes, so the update reaches it as real-time context.

whyRight.text: Prefilling isn't limited to assistant-message continuation — prefixing incoming real-time context, like an advisory update, onto the next message is the documented pattern for injecting mid-conversation updates without restarting anything.

whyWrong.text: Rewriting the system prompt mid-run typically requires rebuilding the session/request setup — a heavier, less direct change than prefixing the update onto the next message.
Sending a separate synthetic user message breaks the natural flow of the review conversation rather than attaching the update to real, ongoing work.
Waiting loses the point of a mid-run update — the goal is factoring in the advisory before this run finishes, not on the next scheduled pass.

questions.stem: The nightly dependency-audit job reviews 30 independent package manifests across the org's services in a single pass. Comments are detailed for the first several manifests, then shrink to one-line 'no issues' notes for the rest — including one manifest with a real license-incompatible dependency the pass missed entirely. What should the team do?
options: Switch to a model with a larger context window so all 30 manifests fit more comfortably.
Reduce the batch to 15 manifests per nightly run to lighten each pass's load.
Restructure into a focused per-manifest pass plus a separate integration pass checking for cross-service inconsistencies.
Instruct the job to 'review every manifest with equal thoroughness' in the prompt.

whyRight.text: Attention dilution across many items in one pass — not context-window size — causes shallow, inconsistent coverage; per-item focused passes plus a separate integration pass restore consistent depth.

whyWrong.text: A larger context window doesn't fix attention quality — more available tokens doesn't mean consistent attention per manifest.
Shrinking the batch size may help somewhat but doesn't structurally fix the root cause — dilution reappears once the per-run count is large enough again.
A prompt instruction to be equally thorough is exactly the kind of proportionate-sounding fix that doesn't survive contact with many items in one pass — probabilistic guidance, not a structural fix.

questions.stem: The team routes the independent second-instance reviewer's findings automatically: any finding it flags immediately blocks the PR. Some flagged issues are genuinely uncertain edge cases a human would want to weigh in on, while others are clear-cut. What change lets downstream routing distinguish these without adding a third review pass?
options: Have the independent reviewer self-report a confidence score alongside each finding, so high-confidence findings auto-block and low-confidence ones route to a human.
Escalate every finding from the independent reviewer to a human, regardless of how clear-cut it looks.
Average the confidence of all findings on a PR into a single PR-level score.
Add a second same-conversation review pass to double-check only the uncertain-looking findings.

whyRight.text: Confidence-calibrated routing — the reviewing instance self-reporting confidence per finding — lets downstream automation auto-act on high-confidence findings while routing low-confidence ones to a human, without adding another pass.

whyWrong.text: Escalating everything defeats the purpose of automating the clear-cut cases and doesn't use the distinction the team is asking for.
A single averaged PR-level score loses the per-finding granularity needed to route individual findings differently.
A second pass in the same conversation still carries the first pass's own reasoning in context — it isn't independent scrutiny, and it's the extra pass the team is trying to avoid.

questions.stem: Each commit on an open PR triggers a fresh `claude -p` invocation to re-review the changed files. A developer replies inline on one finding, 'intentional, ignore this,' then pushes a follow-up commit. The next invocation re-flags the identical finding, with no memory of the developer's reply. An engineer proposes adding a `session_id` so the CLI can look up the earlier exchange itself. Is this the correct diagnosis?
options: Yes — a `session_id` parameter is exactly the missing piece; without it the CLI has nowhere to store the exchange.
No — the pipeline needs a vector database wired in to recall the developer's prior replies.
No — the run has hit a context-window limit from accumulated PR history, dropping the earlier exchange.
No — each `-p` invocation is a separate, stateless call with no memory of prior runs; the harness must explicitly pass the developer's reply into the new prompt.

whyRight.text: The API is fully stateless — every call is independent with no server-side memory. Each fresh `-p` invocation only 'remembers' prior context if the harness explicitly includes it, here the developer's reply, in the new request.

whyWrong.text: No such parameter exists; the API has no session-lookup mechanism — this is the exact fabricated-parameter misconception the corpus documents.
A vector database is for retrieval over long, sprawling histories, not for basic run-to-run memory of one recent reply — a much smaller, simpler problem.
A single developer reply and one follow-up commit is nowhere near a context-window limit — the invocation is stateless from the start, not overflowing.

questions.stem: Over the past year, hundreds of independent CI review sessions have each analyzed a different PR in isolation, with no shared memory between runs. A security lead wants to know whether a specific unsafe-deserialization pattern has ever been flagged before, across any of that history, without manually rereading hundreds of separate review outputs. Which approach most effectively supports this kind of recall?
options: Maintain a single progressively-summarized digest of all findings, updated after every review.
Keep only a rolling window of the most recent 50 reviews' findings.
Use semantic retrieval — embeddings over the archived review history — to retrieve specifically relevant past findings on demand.
Require every finding to carry an exact-match keyword tag and grep the archive for the tag.

whyRight.text: Semantic retrieval over the full archived history retrieves specifically relevant past exchanges on demand — the fix for precise recall from a long, sprawling record that summarization or windowing would compress or discard.

whyWrong.text: A progressively-summarized digest compresses away exactly the specific pattern-level detail this kind of lookup needs.
A rolling window of only the most recent reviews discards most of the year's history the lead needs to search.
Exact-match keyword tagging misses findings described in different wording, since useful recall here depends on meaning, not literal text.

questions.stem: A recruiting pipeline extracts structured candidate records from resumes and application forms. The schema marks `current_employer` required and non-nullable, reasoning every applicant needs one listed. An audit of 6,000 records finds 14% carry a plausible employer name tracing to no real company — those applicants are recent graduates or first-time job seekers with no prior employer. What schema change most directly stops this?
options: Keep the field required, but add a post-extraction lookup that flags employer names unverifiable against a business registry.
Make `current_employer` nullable so the model can return `null` when no employer exists, instead of a value the schema forces it to produce.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model to only fill the field when confident the employer name is accurate.
Replace missing values with a placeholder string like `"N/A"` while keeping the field required and non-nullable.

whyRight.text: Nullable fields let the model return `null` instead of fabricating a value to satisfy a required field — the correct fix when information may be genuinely absent.

whyWrong.text: Post-hoc lookup validation doesn't remove the generation-time pressure that produced the fabrication in the first place — it only catches some of it after the fact.
A prompt instruction asking for confidence-gated filling is probabilistic guidance, not a structural guarantee — the model can still fabricate under required-field pressure.
A placeholder string is still a fabricated non-null value forced by the required field — it doesn't solve the underlying problem, just renames it.

questions.stem: The recruiting pipeline's coordinator has `parsing_agent`, `validation_agent`, and `enrichment_agent` subagent types fully described in its system prompt, each with a clearly scoped role. Engineers notice it never delegates any of the three — it attempts every applicant's full parse-validate-enrich cycle itself in one long response. Its `AgentDefinition` lists only `read_document` among `allowed_tools`. What most reliably fixes this?
options: Rewrite the coordinator's system prompt to explicitly instruct it to delegate to the three subagent types.
Add more detailed descriptions of each subagent's scope to the coordinator's system prompt.
Add `Task` to the coordinator's `allowed_tools` — without it, the coordinator cannot spawn subagents at all.
Increase the coordinator's max_tokens so it has room to reason about when to delegate.

whyRight.text: A coordinator's allowedTools must include Task — without that grant, no amount of prompt wording enables spawning subagents; it's a structural, configuration-level gap.

whyWrong.text: Rewriting the prompt cannot grant a tool the configuration withholds — the prompt cannot compensate for a missing `Task` grant.
The subagent descriptions are already clear and complete; adding more description text doesn't enable spawning when the tool itself is absent.
Token budget has no bearing on whether the coordinator is permitted to call `Task` — this addresses a nonexistent constraint.

questions.stem: Since the pipeline moved to `tool_use` with a strict JSON schema, every extracted record parses cleanly and every field passes its type check. Auditors still occasionally find `years_of_experience` holding a plausible integer that turns out to be the applicant's age, copied from a birthdate line elsewhere in the resume rather than computed from listed job history. What is the most accurate way to interpret this?
options: The schema must be under-constrained — tighten the `years_of_experience` field definition further.
`tool_use` is unreliable for this pipeline; revert to prompt-based JSON requests instead.
This is a syntax error the schema failed to catch and should be reported as a validation bug.
This is expected — `tool_use` eliminated syntax errors, but semantic errors like a value pulled from the wrong source line still require separate validation.

whyRight.text: Strict schemas via tool_use eliminate malformed JSON and wrong-typed fields, but do nothing for content that is schema-valid yet semantically wrong — that class needs business-rule validation and feedback, not schema tightening.

whyWrong.text: No schema constraint can verify a number came from the right source sentence — the field is a valid integer either way, so tightening the schema catches nothing here.
Reverting to prompt-based JSON would reintroduce the syntax-error class tool_use already eliminated, stacked on top of the still-unsolved semantic error.
A schema validator proves only structural validity; a wrong-but-plausible value passes type checking by definition, so this isn't a syntax failure.

questions.stem: A weekly candidate-shortlist digest concatenates all 40 candidates' extracted profiles into one long prompt so a synthesis pass can highlight standout qualifications. It reliably surfaces details for the first and last several candidates, but consistently omits a rare, relevant certification held by a candidate in the middle — even though that candidate's own record correctly includes it. What is the most effective fix?
